pxuyl1: Three past tenses, three different jobs
q9vp6s: When you tell a story, each tense answers a different question. The **imperfect** answers “what was everything like?” and “what did you usually do?”: it describes the place, the weather, the people and habits. The **preterite** answers “what happened?”: it presents finished events, one after another, that move the story forward.
1gjzs52: The **present perfect** answers “what balance do you draw today?”. It looks at the past from the present, with time frames that reach up to now: _hoy, esta semana, este año, ya, todavía no, nunca_. If the time frame is closed (_ayer, el lunes, en 2022, el mes pasado_), most of Spain and almost all of Latin America use the preterite.
jafnu1: A trick to check your text: cover the verbs in the imperfect. If the story still makes sense but has no backdrop, you chose well. If the important events disappear, one of those verbs should have been in the preterite.
1xdp5r6: In some areas (for example, parts of Bolivia, Peru or north-western Argentina) and in spoken Spanish in Spain you will hear more present perfect. For writing, the closed-or-open time frame rule is the safest.

k3thme: Pluperfect: three uses in a story
1auxs8u: **1. Before another past moment.** First you fix a moment with the preterite and then you look back: _Cuando abrí la puerta, mi compañera ya había hecho la cena_. With **ya** you confirm that the earlier thing happened; with **todavía no**, that it had not happened yet.
1ss8jrr: **2. An earlier cause.** You explain a past state or event with something that happened before: _Estaba agotado porque había dormido en el suelo_. It is very useful for apologising or justifying yourself.
lrrcn5: **3. A discovery.** The moment you find out goes in the preterite (_vi, me di cuenta de, supe, descubrí, me enteré de_) and what you discover, which had happened earlier, goes in the pluperfect: _Me di cuenta de que había dejado la cartera en la furgoneta_.
